chunks.text: The banyan (Ficus benghalensis) is an evergreen tree of the fig family Moraceae, native to the Indian subcontinent and found widely in monsoon and rainforest regions of India. It can grow over 30 metres tall and is famous for aerial roots that hang down from its branches; once these reach the ground they thicken into woody secondary trunks, letting a single tree expand its canopy across a huge area without the main trunk itself growing wider. The tree produces figs eaten by birds such as the Indian myna, and fig seeds that pass through a bird's digestive system germinate more readily than seeds that have not — a relationship that helps the tree spread naturally. It is drought-resistant and frost-tolerant, and is rated Least Concern for conservation.

chunks.text: The banyan is the national tree of India and is considered sacred, with temples often built beside old specimens. In Theravada Buddhism it is honoured as the tree under which the Buddha Kassapa is said to have attained enlightenment, and in Jainism it is associated with the first Tirthankara, Adinath, reaching spiritual enlightenment beneath one. Its huge, shady canopy has long made it a natural gathering point for villages. India is home to some of the largest tree canopies on Earth: Thimmamma Marrimanu in Andhra Pradesh covers about 19,107 square metres of canopy, the largest known by that measure, while the Great Banyan in the Acharya Jagadish Chandra Bose Indian Botanic Garden near Kolkata covers roughly 18,918 square metres and is about 250 years old. Historically, the Kabirvad banyan on the Narmada River was said to be able to shelter thousands of people beneath it.
